Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Review the pathophysiology of diabetic neuropathy.
Discuss the pathophysiology of diabetic vascular disease.
Explain how to diagnose diabetic vascular disease and neuropathy.
Differentiate Charcot arthropathy from infection.
Pathophysiology of Diabetic Neuropathy
Overview
Diabetic neuropathy manifests in the somatic and/or autonomic parts of the peripheral
nervous system.

Of all patients with diabetes mellitus, 10% have some form of sensory, motor, or autonomic
dysfunction at the time of diagnosis; neuropathy develops in 50% to 75% of these patients
within 25 years of diagnosis.1
No single etiologic pathway has been confirmed as responsible for all diabetic neuropathy.
Metabolic factors (glycosylation of proteins, reduced availability of nerve growth factors, and
immunologic factors) in combination with a microvascular insufficiency likely result in the final
common pathway of neuropathic changes.2

Overview
Diabetic peripheral neuropathy is the most common form of peripheral neuropathy,
affecting 30% to 50% of all patients with diabetes mellitus. It is caused by vascular and
metabolic pathways. Neurons require glucose for normal function; however, chronic
hyperglycemia leads to oxidative stress on the neuron by increased production of
oxidative species, lipid peroxidation and protein nitrosylation, and diminished levels of
glutathione and ascorbate. Analysis of the nutrient vessels in patients with diabetes
mellitus who have neuropathy demonstrates microangiopathy with thickened basement
membrane, endothelial cell proliferation, and decreased oxygen tension compared with
patients with diabetes mellitus who do not have neuropathy.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Nerves
Sensory neuropathy
Sensory neuropathy is the most prevalent and obvious nerve dysfunction observed in
patients with diabetes mellitus, affecting as many as 70%.
In a study by Reiber et al,3 the critical triad of sensory neuropathy, trauma, and foot
deformity was present in 63% of patients with lower extremity ulcers.
Pain is associated with 25% to 33% of neuropathies. The pain may be superficial (burning,
tingling, or allodynia), shooting or electric-like, or cramping and aching.4
Sensory disturbances show a length-related pattern, with stocking and glove distribution
from a dying-back distal axonopathy.

Sensory neuropathy can be assessed via the Semmes-Weinstein monofilament test.
Protective sensation is indicated by the ability to perceive a 5.07 (10 g) monofilament applied
perpendicular to the skin.
Motor neuropathy
Motor neuropathy is most clinically apparent in the foot, as evidenced by the development of
claw toes from intrinsic muscle weakness and equinus contracture of the Achilles tendon.
These factors transfer stress to the forefoot, resulting in focal high pressures and resultant
skin breakdown.
Claw toes occur because of the dysfunction of intrinsic muscles that cause hyperextension of
the metatarsophalangeal joints and flexion of the proximal and distal interphalangeal joints.
Skin compromise occurs secondary to pressure placed on the dorsal surface as the toes
contact the toe box of the shoe and increased pressure occurs beneath the metatarsal
heads. Achilles tendon contracture displaces excessive pressure to the front of the foot,
resulting in increased risk of ulceration.
Autonomic neuropathy
Autonomic neuropathy is the most overlooked manifestation of peripheral neuropathy. It
occurs if the autonomic system cannot control the blood vessel tone and the sweat (eccrine
and apocrine) glands in the foot.
Sweat gland dysfunction allows the skin to dry out and crack, allowing the ingress of
microbes.
Standing foot pressure may be as high as 400 kPa, which necessitates fine regulation of the
blood vessels to ensure adequate oxygenation of tissues and avoid local anoxia.6

Nerves
Sensory neuropathy primarily is caused by injury to small nerve fibers that sense pain
and temperature. It usually manifests early in patients with diabetes mellitus and
commonly results in cramping and burning pain. As the condition progresses, loss of
pain and temperature sensation occur. Not all patients have pain; however, most
patients will have some manifestation of neuropathic pain, such as burning, tingling, or
electric pain. The symptoms may become worse at night, leading to difficulty sleeping.
The pattern is symmetric loss of sensation beginning distally and progressing proximally.

Large nerve fibers are affected later in the disease process, impairing proprioception
and light touch.5
Autonomic neuropathy can affect multiple organ systems, such as cardiovascular,
gastrointestinal, sexual, and even hyperhidrosis or hypohidrosis. The dysregulation of
the vascular system leads to arteriovenous shunting. The loss of the C fiber pain
response leads to disruption of the nerve axon vasodilation response that causes
vasodilation and increased permeability of the vascularity. This decreased blood flow to
areas of trauma is the reason ulcers and infections in patients with diabetes mellitus
may not present with the inflammation normally expected.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
History of type 1 or type 2 diabetes mellitus or prediabetes mellitus
Pain at rest or at night that is not resolved with mobilization
Increasing difficulty with balance
Dry cracking skin on the feet
Physical Examination
Gross examination of the condition of the skin. Dry, cracked skin, callus formation, or
ulcerations may be signs of neuropathy.
Bilateral hammertoe deformity and decreased Achilles tendon reflex
Semmes-Weinstein 5.07 nylon monofilament testing
Vibratory sensation in the lower extremities with the use of a 128-Hz tuning fork, which has
been shown to have a lower threshold for detecting impaired sensation compared with
monofilament testing.4

The patient history and physical examination are low-cost, high-yield screening
modalities for diabetic peripheral neuropathy. They can be completed quickly.
Commonly, decreased sensation is patchy, and the dorsal and plantar aspects of the foot
must be assessed.
Diabetic Vasculopathy
Pathophysiology
Atherosclerosis is secondary endothelial injury, smooth muscle cell proliferation, foam cell
development and infiltration, platelet activation, and increased inflammation.1
Most commonly affects the deep femoral artery and those distal to the knee
Microvascular disease is not secondary to occlusion of the arteries but a result of diabetes
mellitus changing the vessels themselves by changing the flow in capillary beds and the
normal function of the endothelium inhibiting the response to inflammation and injury.

Pathophysiology
The effect of diabetes mellitus and chronic hyperglycemia is observed in larger vessels
and the smaller end vasculature. In the larger arteries, atherosclerosis forms in the same
inflammatory pathway observed in patients without diabetes mellitus. Additional effects
of diabetes mellitus on the peripheral vasculature include vascular smooth muscle cell
dysfunction and alterations in platelet function and fibrinolysis that lead to a
hypercoagulable state, further potentiating atherogenesis.
Microvascular disease is not secondary to occlusion of the microvasculature but a
complex interaction between metabolic changes in the endothelial lining that decreases
permeability and neuropathy, causing interruption in the vascular flow2 (Figure 1).

Figure 1: Illustrations show the development of atherosclerotic plaque with
superimposed thrombus. A, An artery contains three layers: the inner intima, the media,
and the outer layer of the adventitia. B, The initial steps of atherosclerosis include
adhesion of blood leukocytes to the activated endothelial monolayer; directed migration
of the bound leukocytes into the intima; and maturation of monocytes (the most
numerous of the leukocytes recruited) into macrophages and their uptake of lipid,
yielding foam cells. C, Lesion progression involves the migration of smooth muscle cells
(SMCs) from the media to the intima; the proliferation of resident intimal SMCs and
media-derived SMCs; and the heightened synthesis of extracellular matrix
macromolecules, such as collagen, elastin, and proteoglycans. Plaque macrophages and
SMCs can die in advancing lesions, some via apoptosis. Extracellular lipid derived from
dead and dying cells can accumulate in the central region of a plaque, often denoted the
lipid or necrotic core. Advancing plaques also contain cholesterol crystals and
microvessels. D, Thrombosis, the ultimate complication of atherosclerosis, often
complicates a physical disruption of the atherosclerotic plaque. A fracture of the fibrous
cap of the plaque has enabled blood coagulation components to come into contact with
tissue factors in the interior of the plaque, triggering the thrombus that extends into the
vessel lumen, the location at which it can impede blood flow. (Reproduced with
permission from Libby P, Ridker PM, Hansson GK: Progress and challenges in translating
the biology of atherosclerosis. Nature 2011;473[7347]:317-325.)

Clinical Examination
Palpation of dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial artery pulses
Test capillary refill of the digits (should be less than 2 seconds)
Examination for skin discoloration
Venous stasis
Darkening of the skin
Examine for hair on the legs/feet because alopecia may be an indication of poor vascularity of
the extremity (Figure 2)
Figure 2: Medial (A) and lateral (B) view clinical photographs show a foot with poor vascularity.
Note the darkened, thickened skin. The lesser toes demonstrate severe ischemia. (Courtesy of
Lew Schon, MD, Baltimore, MD.)


Clinical Examination
Changes that occur secondary to vasculopathy occur over a long period of time. Subtle
changes usually are not even noticed by the patient. The danger is that the body
accommodates to these changes to maintain an equilibrium. Often, a patient has a
normal appearance; however, a subtle trauma can disrupt the equilibrium. A simple cut
while clipping toenails or a minor blister or ulcer can begin a cascade that leads to
severe consequences. Therefore, a quick assessment of vascular status may prevent
adverse events.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Calcified arteries are visible on plain radiographs of the foot and ankle.
Computed Tomography
CT angiography can be performed to map out the lower extremity arteries to determine
occlusions in a noninvasive manner.
Disadvantage is the need for contrast, which is known to be nephrotoxic in patients who
already are at risk for substantial renal disease.
Ultrasonography
Arterial Doppler can measure the patency and flow of lower extremity vessels.
Magnetic Resonance Arthrography
Compared with angiography, magnetic resonance arthrography has a sensitivity as high as
99.5% and a specificity of 98.8% for detecting hemodynamically substantial stenosis.5
Diagnosis

Ankle-brachial index (ABI) is a more reliable measure of peripheral disease than simple
palpation of pulses.
ABI is the ratio of the systolic pressure in the ankle divided by the systolic pressure measured
in the arm.
ABI between 1.3 and 0.9 is normal.
ABI less than 0.9 is indicative of obstruction.
ABI higher than 1.3 is indicative of calcific artery disease, making the arteries
uncompressible.
Toe pressure is less susceptible to abnormal results from arterial calcification.
Toe pressure higher than 30 mm Hg indicates adequate perfusion for wound healing.6
Transcutaneous oxygen measurement may be a predictor of wound-healing ability.
Values less than 25 mm Hg pose substantial impairment to wound healing even with
hyperbaric therapy.7
Values higher than 75 mm Hg are associated with excellent wound healing.8
Angiography: Digital subtraction angiography is the most accurate method to evaluate
circulation of the lower extremity and the only method that can be used to diagnose and
manage the condition at the same time.
Charcot Arthropathy Versus Infection
Infection and acute Charcot arthropathy often are confused in the clinical setting because they
result in similar symptoms.
Swollen, erythematous foot
Increased pain in the extremity
Presence of an ulcer and deformity
Charcot arthropathy
Rubor decreases with elevation.
Lack of systemic symptoms, such as fever, chills, loss of glycemic control
44% of patients have a concomitant ulcer with initial presentation of Charcot arthropathy.9
Advanced imaging studies
Plain radiographs may not help distinguish acute Charcot arthropathy from
osteomyelitis/infection because they result in similar destructive bone changes.
MRI and nuclear medicine studies may be useful to distinguish between the two pathologies.
Three-phase techneitum-99m scintigraphy in combination with indium-111–labeled
leukocyte scintigraphy is the most specific modality for differentiating infection from Charcot

arthropathy.
MRI is the best imaging modality for differentiating Charcot arthropathy from soft-tissue


Charcot Arthropathy Versus Infection
Plain radiographs are 50% specific in detecting osteomyelitis. Although plain radiography
is a critical imaging modality for characterizing deformity and the Eichenholtz stage of
Charcot arthropathy, it is not ideal for ruling out infection. If superimposed osteomyelitis
or soft-tissue abscess is suspected, advanced imaging studies may be helpful. MRI and
bone scintigraphy are options. Three-phase techneitum-99m scintigraphy in
combination with indium-111–labeled leukocyte scintigraphy is associated with a
sensitivity of 93% to 100% and a specificity of approximately 80%.4 Studies suggest that
MRI is less specific than the combination of three-phase techneitum-99m and indium-
111–labeled leukocyte scintigraphy for detecting osteomyelitis.10 MRI, with its excellent
soft-tissue resolution, is superior to bone scanning with regard to ruling out associated
soft-tissue abscess.
